I went to watch it in the theater with a friend. 5 minutes in, I could see that this was a well acted, well written movie… and absolutely not something that either of us wanted to watch. I’ve only walked out of three movies in my life, and hearing from other people what happens later in the film, I’m glad I walked out of it when I did. I get why people like it, but I don’t want to put myself in that headspace watching a movie.

It's an incredible movie, and one that my partner and I have reference surprisingly often, there are so many memorable and darkly hysterical lines and deliveries in there, "pump pump pump," "there's blood in my BM," "SCAB!!" and so on.

It also begins with the most unbelievable set of monologues. Jon Lovitz's righteous breakup at the restaurant, followed right away by Philip Seymour Hoffman's amazingly humdrum ramblings about his sexual fantasies and utter self-hatred. The whole film is just an outstanding panorama of pent-up misery and repression and desperation.

I feel as though that the pretense/reputation of the film is greater than its made out to be nowadays. That is to say, the reason why Happiness was so dark was due to the cultural context it which it was released. Perhaps I'm jaded by the films I've watched and am now just used to it, but I sincerely doubt modern audiences would find Happiness as unappealing as the audience of its own time. In fact, a lot gratuity can be easily accessible through Netflix or even YouTube. In other words: is it really still as disturbing as you make it out or is it just that it's "more fun" to watch with the "taboo" feeling in mind? Even watching it as a teenager, I found it much less disturbing than Ichi the Killer or Silence of the Lambs.

I can see that point, in fact I think you may be correct when I consider the cultural impact of the internet and the “shock videos” from people who want clout. 

However I think there is a certain mixture of factors, one of the largest factors being the cast and timing. I think the timing of the scenes and dialogue is something you can’t replicate with the conveyor belt of content produced for Netflix and YouTube. Creators are racing to shovel content on to their platforms, due to the fact that they can’t take their time (mainly due to the damaged attention spans of most content consumers these days and needing to stay relevant) they greatly sacrifice timing. Parts of Happiness make you feel like you’re peeking in the window of someone’s life, and you 100% shouldn’t be watching it. And all while YouTube can produce content like that, I feel it’s more of a “Jesus, what the fuck, I shouldn’t be watching this, that’s enough internet for today.” Not something that I wake up the next day thinking about. 

I tried to draw the analogy with McDonald’s. Almost all streaming platforms are guilty of this, but Netflix and YouTube are like the McDonald’s of movie streaming. They only allow what they think is appropriate. It’s familiar, quick, easily accessible. It’s simultaneously more than what you need, but somehow lacks substance. It lacks the time, thought and effort. 

I think after the 90s and the creation of internet streaming platforms has greatly damaged not just good storytelling in film, but also the audience and how we consume the material.

I feel like I might have come off more disparaging of the movie than I intended, and for some reason the edit option isn’t showing up for me to append my post. I’m not suggesting that there’s anything *wrong* with the movie or anyone who enjoyed it, I’m just sharing my personal reaction. While I’m fine watching movies that push boundaries, shock and make me feel uncomfortable, I’ve also discovered that there are limits to what content I’m willing to sit through regardless of quality or intention, and Happiness was one of the films that showed me where those limits were. I think in a way I’m saying that *because* it was so well done, it hit me more than other films covering similar territory, and it just made me feel sick to my stomach, depressed, and like I wanted to wash my brain out - within 10 minutes. As I said, I get why people think it’s a great movie, but I had to bow out.
Fair enough. Well said.

>At the end of KOTFM it feels like Marty is apologizing for what he just subjected us to. I understand the impulse, but you can't actually do that.

Yeah lol same as the Dahmer series. "Isn't it terrible how people exploit this tragedy for money, like we just did? Anyways we are different because we admit it."

> At the end of KOTFM it feels like Marty is apologizing for what he just subjected us to. I understand the impulse, but you can't actually do that.

I think that's a flattening take okn that penultimate scene. I think there's a lot of complexity in there. It's an acknowledgment of how this tale (and by extension, similar tales) were treated in the past. White actors voicing Native Americans, a tidy crime narrative, played for cheesy entertainment. In a way it's an argument *for* Marty's film, quite the opposite of an apology.

At the same time, it's an acknowledgment of the shortcomings of dramatic filmmaking. Marty is also saying, "Look — what I'm doing is fundamentally the same thing." You see much of the craft of moviemaking there. Actors reading from scripts, the score, sound effects, etc. I wouldn't frame this as an apology. It's an expression of humility.

And yet, per the first point, it's almost a brag at the same time. It walks a really interesting line.
